newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE-Battle rages for soul of Jewish state.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Battle rages for soul of Jewish state.

text.p: In a war for the soul of the Jewish state, American Jews and Israel's powerful Orthodox rabbis have escalated the battle over who is a Jew.

Conversions performed in Israel by Judaism's two main lenient streams have never been valid here, where it takes the blessing of an Orthodox rabbi to make a marriage or divorce official or label a food product kosher.

So when Reform Jews -- rebelling against a so-called religious status quo in place since the establishment of the Jewish state -- sued in Israel's high court to have their converts recognised, the rabbis fought back.

They proposed a law to codify the longstanding but informal ban on all but their own conversions. Converts from abroad would still be recognised as Jews -- an arrangement that never threatened the supremacy of Orthodox rabbis over their more liberal counterparts within Israel.
The Reform and Conservative movements in the United States, which are trying to make inroads in Israel, cried foul and said the law would be an insult to non-Orthodox Jews everywhere.
NETANYAHU TRYING TO FORGE A COMPROMISE
Experts say a deal engineered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to quell the uproar in the United States, where as in Israel most Jews are not Orthodox, will not end the crisis.

"At a time when they hoped to be celebrating the 50th anniversary of Israel, they're talking instead about differences of opinion, and are they really the same people," said Bernie Moscovitz, chief of operations for America's United Jewish Appeal.
American Jews, 93 percent of whom belong to the rejected Reform and Conservative branches, send hundreds of millions of dollars to Israel each year.
If Israel will not recognise their converts, they say, they can always send their money elsewhere.
"What this is essentially saying is there are second-class Jews," Moscovitz said.
The Orthodox counter that those converted by Reform or Conservative rabbis are not inferior Jews -- but simply Gentiles.

Netanyahu promised to support the legislation when he made coalition deals with religious political parties that help keep his government in power. But he also does not want to alienate U.S. Jews, and worked to freeze the bill in parliament.

With the legislation now on hold and in hopes of a compromise, Reform Jews have postponed their lawsuits until mid-August. Talks have begun between Reform and Conservative Jews and the government. The Orthodox have refused to sign up.
SOVIET EXODUS MADE IDENTITY PROBLEM MORE ACUTE

"The Reform (Jews), some of the rabbis even, don't believe in God. They would marry a Jew and a non-Jew. They would go further. They would marry people who are the same sex," Orthodox Rabbi Avraham Ravitz told Reuters.
"They are a subculture. They are not a religion. To them, Judaism is like a club, something you can join just because you want to," said Ravitz, who represents the United Torah Party in parliament.

A Jewish exodus from the former Soviet Union at the end of the Cold War brought 200,000 Russians to Israel who by law cannot be classified as Jews, said Rabbi Donniel Hartman of the progressive Shalom Hartman Institute.
Under ritual Jewish law, anyone with a Jewish mother is a Jew, but some of the immigrants have only Jewish fathers.

"If the Russians are interested only in Reform or Conservative Judaism, and it's the first time in five generations anyone from that family has stepped into a synagogue, how can the state not allow this to be recognised?" Moscovitz asked.
Reform Rabbis say interest in their conversions is also high among families who want to convert their adopted children and Gentiles who want to marry Jews.

And at a time when American Jewish culture is experiencing a rebirth and non-Orthodox Jewish day schools are filling up, this is not the time to reject American versions of Judaism, said Moscovitz, whose organisation sent Israel $300 million last year.
"American Jews care about this country and believe it is central to their existence as Jews. The fact that they're not living here doesn't make them any less caring," he said.
For Israel to maintain a leadership role in world Jewry, he said, its actions will have to change.
"For the diaspora Jews, Israel is the conduit of their memory. It is through Israel that they go back to their grandparents who said, 'Next year in Jerusalem,'" Hartman said.
"The tragedy is that Israelis don't even understand this," he said.
